sense: two of a kind taken together

terms.grammar: noun, third declension, neuter; plural paria
evidence: Cic. Lael. 15: tria aut quattuor … paria amīcōrum
Traupman 113, 356: pār soccōrum, duo paria digitālium
terms.comment: The neuter noun of the adjective pār, “equal” (see equal): two that match, of animals, things or people (a pair of friends, of gladiators, of brothers). Things that come in pairs are often simply plural in Latin: calceī are shoes or a pair of shoes; pār is used when the pairs are counted (Traupman 114: duo paria digitālium).

terms.gloss: two at a time, two each; two (with plural-only nouns)
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.14.2: distribuit bīnōs singulīs patribus familiārum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Att. 6.1.9: bīnae (litterae), two letters (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In pairs, two to each. With a noun used only in the plural, or with a different sense there, it stands for duo: bīnae litterae are two letters (epistles), duae litterae two letters of the alphabet (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: ex omnibus saeculīs vix tria aut quattuor nōminantur paria amīcōrum
phrases.english: from all the ages hardly three or four pairs of friends are named

phrases.latin: Quīntī prōgeniēs Arrī, pār nōbile frātrum
phrases.english: the sons of Quintus Arrius, a famous pair of brothers
